source.title: Predictive Model Degrees of Freedom in Linear Regression
source.authors: Bo Luan; Yoonkyung Lee; Yun-Zhang Zhu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper is present. Figure content is partly flattened, so plotted numerical values are not extractable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent in linear least-squares regression rather than deep networks, and examines whether plotting risk against a different complexity measure changes the curve.
record.gate_note: The paper's own least-squares risk curves and risk plotted against predictive model degrees of freedom are recorded below. Results cited from other studies and numerical results about selecting models by risk estimators are not recorded as claim results.
record.test_reason: The paper reproduces model-wise double descent in minimum-norm least-squares subset regression. Its central argument is that re-indexing risk by a proposed effective complexity measure (predictive model degrees of freedom, df_R) turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped bias-variance curve. That is a specific restating of the claim along V7's lines. Neither original source is this paper.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. The authors propose predictive model degrees of freedom for linear procedures. They argue that indexing least-squares risk by df_R, treating OLS and minimum-norm least squares as separate procedures, reconciles double descent with the classical bias-variance trade-off. Most of the paper, however, concerns risk estimation and model selection, where their criterion favours more parsimonious models than Cp, AIC or cross-validation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses subset least-squares regression and a predictive-degrees-of-freedom reparameterization, rather than a deep-network size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The risk-versus-complexity presentation distinguishes the underparameterized and overparameterized regimes; Figure 6 uses variables added in descending coefficient order.

fits_no_version.finding: In ridge regression, df_R is decreasing in λ. In 1-NN, linear, quadratic and cosine interpolators and in interpolating splines, df_R differs among interpolating models (e.g. df_R/n of 1, 0.833, 0.867, 0.863).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective complexity measures can differentiate interpolating models that share zero training error.

record.problems: The claim-related curves are presented as figures without extractable numerical values or reported uncertainty. The tested model class is linear least squares, not deep networks or other model classes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results left out. The paper's other analyses of prediction-error estimators and interpolating-model initialization do not test the listed double-descent versions.

untested.parts: Sample size is not varied near the threshold.
Only least-squares linear regression with a model-size axis. Other model classes (kernels, trees, networks) are not tested.
No test of whether one complexity measure predicts peak location across axes.
Label noise, multiple peaks and optimally tuned regularization are not examined. Ridge appears only for df_R versus λ, not risk.
Only linear least squares on the model-size axis. Other effective-parameter counts, other model classes, and epoch or sample axes are not tested.

missing.what: Theorem 4.4 and Remark 4.2 show df_R decreases in p beyond n for isotropic features. A simulation with random correlation matrices gives the fraction of steps with df_R non-increasing as 0.9839. This is the mechanism behind the V7 re-indexing.
Asymptotic df_R ≈ n/2 + (n/2)·min(p,n)/|n−p| diverges at p = n, and df_R < df_F for p > 2n (equicorrelated features).

The average true out-of-sample prediction error across p (n = 50, d = 120, linear and nonlinear mean, sparse κ = 5) is plotted through and past the interpolation threshold. The shape is not described in the text.

record.verdict_notes: The double-descent evidence is a single illustrative simulation (Figure 6, largely duplicated by Figure 1), with no numbers or uncertainty. The re-indexing claim rests on a figure plus the df_R monotonicity results. I changed the tranche from T2 to T5 because the paper's contribution is an argument that the second descent is an artifact of the complexity axis. I dropped the V5 link, since peak-location prediction across axes is not addressed.

versions.untested_parts: Changing sample size near the interpolation threshold.
Only least-squares linear regression is examined; other model classes are not tested.
The predictive-complexity reparameterization is examined for model size only, not epochs or sample size.
No systematic test of label-noise dependence, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
The paper examines its proposed predictive degrees of freedom in a least-squares setting, not alternative effective-parameter counts or other model classes.

rows.subject: least squares method in subset regression

rows.value: figure only; the text says the double-descent phenomenon is observed
rows.note: The text describes the plotted prediction error as showing double descent.
rows.check: The text states double descent is observed against subset size p, but the result is figure only. Variables are added prescient (descending-coefficient) order, following Belkin et al. 2019's setting. It covers one linear model class only.

rows.subject: least squares method in subset regression
rows.operation_detail: Plots the same prediction error against the logarithm of predictive model degrees of freedom, separately for the underparameterized and overparameterized regimes.
rows.measure: Out-of-sample prediction error against log(predictive model degrees of freedom)
rows.value: figure only; the text says the two side-by-side U-shaped curves become two similar U-shaped curves over a comparable complexity range
rows.note: Supports reparameterizing the size-axis curve with predictive degrees of freedom; the authors show separate curves for the two regimes rather than one ordinary U-shaped curve.
rows.check: r3 should not link to V5. The paper does not test whether one complexity measure predicts the peak location across size, epochs and samples. For V7, the authors explicitly say double descent is 'well reconciled' with the classical trade-off when risk is plotted against df_R. However, this requires plotting the under- and overparameterized regimes as separate procedures (two U-curves), not one single U-curve. Figure only.
